questions.topic: Edges of a polygonal prism from its vertex count
questions.learningObjective: recover the base polygon of a prism from its vertex count and count its edges
questions.stem: A prism has two parallel congruent polygonal bases joined by a band of parallelogram side faces, and every edge of one base joins one edge of the other. If the whole solid has 20 vertices, how many edges does it have? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Let n be the number of sides of the base. Each base has n vertices, so the prism has 2n of them, and 2n = 20 gives n = 10. Edges come in three groups: n around the bottom base, n around the top base, and n lateral edges joining them, so the total is 3n = 30. Counting the three groups separately gives 10 + 10 + 10, which is again 30. Euler's formula checks the count: a prism has F = n + 2 = 12 faces, and 20 - 30 + 12 = 2, the value every convex polyhedron must give.
questions.hint: The vertex count is twice the number of sides of the base, and each base edge also produces one lateral edge.

The single cube at the centre of the layer is removed, cutting a 1 by 1 square tunnel straight through from the bottom face to the top face; the four cubes at the corners and the four cubes at the edge middles all stay. Count an edge of the solid only where two of its faces meet, so the eight square seams inside the two ring-shaped horizontal faces are not edges. How many edges does the remaining solid have?

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Why Euler's formula holds for a convex polyhedron
questions.learningObjective: prove Euler's formula for convex polyhedra
questions.stem: Prove that any convex polyhedron with V vertices, E edges and F faces satisfies V - E + F = 2, and explain why the same count does not apply unchanged to a solid with a tunnel through it.

answer.exemplar: The cleanest route is induction on the number of faces, and the key move is to delete one edge together with one face. Take a convex polyhedron whose surface is a closed piece of the sphere, so it is homeomorphic to a sphere and stays that way after the surgery below. If it has the smallest possible number of faces, it is the tetrahedron, and 4 - 6 + 4 = 2, so the base case is done. Otherwise choose an edge e. It is the common edge of exactly two faces F1 and F2. Because the solid is convex, F1 and F2 are the only two faces that meet along e, and merging them into a single face leaves a closed surface with the same vertex set, one edge fewer and one face fewer. Hence V - E + F is unchanged by the step: subtracting one from E and one from F leaves the total alone. Repeating until only the tetrahedron is left, the value must still be 2. That also explains the tunnel case. A solid with a tunnel has a surface homeomorphic to a torus, not a sphere, and the same surgery can never reduce it to a tetrahedron; the smallest such solid, a solid torus, gives V - E + F = 0, and a solid with g tunnels gives 2 - 2g. The general rule is that the answer is 2 minus twice the number of tunnels, so the formula is a statement about the shape of the surface, not about arithmetic.

questions.explanation: Euler's formula is a statement about the shape of the surface rather than about arithmetic on counts, and the proof turns on a surgery that leaves the quantity alone. Deleting one edge merges exactly two faces into one, so the edge count and the face count each fall by one while the vertex count is untouched, and the value of V - E + F does not move. Iterating that surgery reduces any convex polyhedron to the tetrahedron, whose counts are 4, 6 and 4 and whose value is 2, so every convex polyhedron gives 2. A solid with a tunnel is the case where the surgery cannot finish, because the surface is a torus rather than a sphere; the smallest such solid gives 0, and g tunnels give 2 - 2g. Notice also that the two negative signs in the formula are load bearing: the formula is not symmetric in V and F, so writing it as V + F - E is a different and false statement.
questions.hint: Delete an edge and merge its two faces; the quantity V - E + F does not change, so reduce to the tetrahedron.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Why each tessellation angle must divide 360
questions.learningObjective: explain why the angles at a tessellation vertex must sum to a full turn
questions.stem: Explain why a shape that tiles the plane edge to edge must have every interior angle divide 360 exactly, and why the condition is not automatic. Use the equilateral triangle of side 1 and the regular pentagon of side 1 as your two examples.

answer.exemplar: At any vertex of an edge-to-edge tiling the corners that meet there fill a full turn, so their interior angles add to exactly 360 degrees, and a full turn is a fixed total. Because the tiling repeats and every corner of the shape is used, the same angle appears at many vertices, and at each of them a whole number of copies of it is packed into the same 360, so the angle must be 360 over a whole number. That is the definition of dividing 360, and it is not automatic: the equilateral triangle has interior angle 60, and 360 over 60 is 6, so six corners of it fit round every point, which is exactly what the triangular tiling does. The regular pentagon has interior angle 108, and 360 over 108 is 3 and a third, so three corners give 324 and leave a 36 degree gap while four corners overshoot at 432; no arrangement of pentagon corners closes a full turn, which is why the regular pentagon cannot tile the plane on its own. A second example is the regular heptagon, whose interior angle is 128.57, and 360 over 128.57 is not a whole number either. So among the regular polygons only the triangle, the square and the hexagon pass the test, which is why exactly three of the eleven regular polygons tile the plane.

questions.explanation: The key sentence is that the corners meeting at a vertex fill exactly 360 degrees, so a whole number of the shape's interior angle must fit into a full turn. Every shape that tiles the plane has its corners meeting other corners in this way, and the full turn is a fixed quantity, so the angle must be 360 over a whole number. The equilateral triangle illustrates the rule working: 360 over 60 is 6, and six corners really do close up round each point. The regular pentagon illustrates it failing: 360 over 108 is 3.3333, so three corners total 324 and leave a 36 degree gap, and four corners overshoot. The condition is not automatic because nothing forces a shape's angle to be a divisor of a full turn; most angles are not, and that is why only three of the eleven regular polygons tile the plane.
questions.hint: Corners at a vertex must fill 360 degrees exactly, so a whole number of them must fit.

questions.topic: Why an oblique prism has the volume of a right one
questions.learningObjective: explain why shearing a prism does not change its volume
questions.stem: A prism with a parallelogram base can be tilted so that its side edges lean, and it is still called a prism. Explain why the tilted prism has the same volume as the upright one with the same base and height, using slices parallel to the base.

answer.exemplar: Slice the solid with planes parallel to the base. In an upright prism every such slice is a copy of the base, so each slice has the area of the base and the total volume is that area times the perpendicular height. In the tilted prism the slices are not the base polygon but translate copies of it, slid sideways as the cut moves up, and a translation preserves area exactly, so every slice still has the area of the base. The volume is the sum of the slice areas times the thickness of each slice, that is the base area times the perpendicular distance from the base to the top face, which is the height, and the perpendicular height is unchanged by tilting because the top face stays parallel to the base and the distance between two parallel planes does not depend on where you look. The same idea is Cavalieri's principle: two solids whose cross sections by a family of parallel planes agree have equal volumes, and here the two prisms have equal cross sections, so they have equal volumes. Shearing a prism is a shear of the whole solid, and a shear is exactly the motion that leaves every parallel slice congruent to itself.

questions.explanation: The decisive point is that a slice parallel to the base of a tilted prism is a translated copy of the base, not a different shape. Translation preserves area, so each slice has the base area whether the prism leans or not, and adding the slice areas times their thicknesses gives base area times the perpendicular height. Tilting does not change that perpendicular height, because the top face stays parallel to the base and the distance between parallel planes is fixed. This is Cavalieri's principle in a concrete case: two solids with matching cross sections in every parallel plane have equal volumes, so the oblique prism and the right prism with the same base and height have the same volume.

questions.stem: A solid is made by stacking a right square prism of base side 3 and height 4 on top of a square pyramid of base side 3 and height 6, the two sharing the same 3 by 3 base outline. What is the total volume of the solid? Give the value to 4 decimal places.
questions.explanation: Split the solid where the prism and pyramid meet, and add the two volumes. The prism has base area 3 times 3, that is 9, and height 4, so its volume is 9 times 4, that is 36. The pyramid has the same base area 9 and height 6, so its volume is one third of 9 times 6, that is 18. The total is 36 + 18, that is 54. The check that the split is fair: the prism and the pyramid have the same base, so the solid is exactly the union of the two with an overlap of zero area, and an independent slice calculation agrees. Slicing at height t above the shared base, the area of the slice is 9 up to height 6, and the volume is the integral of those areas, that is 9 times 6 plus 9 times 4, that is 54 again.
questions.hint: Add the volume of the prism, base times height, to one third of base times height for the pyramid.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Faces of the rhombic dodecahedron that fills space with cubes
questions.learningObjective: count the faces of the space-filling partner of the cube
questions.stem: Cubes cannot fill space on their own, but each cube fits exactly against a solid whose twelve faces are congruent rhombi, and the two shapes together fill all of space. How many faces does that second solid have? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The partner of the cube in the space-filling pair is the rhombic dodecahedron, and the name already records the count: it has twelve faces. Counting them from the shape also works. Take a cube of side 2, whose corners sit at the eight points with coordinates plus or minus 1, and add a square pyramid of height 1 on each of its six faces, so the six new apices sit on the coordinate axes at distance 2 from the centre. The slant edge from such an apex to a corner of its base is the square root of 1 plus 1 plus 1, that is 1.7321, and each of the four edges of a side face is one of those slant edges, so every side face is a rhombus. Each of the 6 pyramids contributes 4 rhombi, and each is shared with a neighbouring pyramid, so the solid has 6 times 4 divided by 2, that is 12 faces. Euler's formula agrees: the 8 cube corners and the 6 apices give 14 vertices, and with 24 edges, 14 - 24 + 12 gives 2. One face checked by hand holds the two cube corners (0 minus 1, 0 minus 1, 0 minus 1) and (1, 0 minus 1, 0 minus 1) with the apices (0, minus 2, 0) and (0, 0, minus 2), all in the plane y + z = minus 2, and there the four slant sides are each 1.7321 while the diagonals are 2 and 2.8284, which is consistent because 1 plus 2 equals 3, the square of the side.
questions.hint: Build it from a cube with a pyramid of height 1 on each of its six faces, and count the shared rhombi once.
